blocks.text: What the ברבורים אבוסים, fattened barburim, at the table of Solomon were, 1 Reg. IV, 23. [var. V, 3.].

As with the Roman ancilia, so in the various interpretations of the word ברבורים barburim in 1 Reg. IV, 23. [var. V, 3.], the false ones have been fashioned so closely to resemble the true that it is not easy to tell the one from the other. From an inspection of the passage itself it is clear that the ברבורי׳ barburim are listed among the animals that were consumed daily at the table of Solomon. For the sacred text reads: And the provisions of Solomon for each day were ten oxen, etc., besides harts, and roebucks, and buffaloes, ברבורים אבוסים, and fattened barburim. Junius and Mercerus explain this as all the choicest animals. Apuleius would have said pastus electiles [choice fare], as in book 10 of the Metamorphoses: Nor could the ass, who alone was present, be affected by such food, and yet every day the choice fare was nowhere to be found. The Greek interpreters were of the same opinion; two versions of theirs survive. One has ἐκλεκτῶν σιτευτὰ [eklektōn siteuta], the other ὀρνίθων ἐκλεκτῶν νομάδων [ornithōn eklektōn nomadōn]. But in both ἐκλεκτῶν [eklektōn] stands for ברבר׳ barburim, and in the second they supply ὀρνίθων [ornithōn] on their own. As if choice fattened birds were meant, and these of the gallinaceous kind. For that is what ὄρνιθες [ornithes] are in that passage, as we proved above ^{a)}. So too the Talmudists, in the tractate Bava Metsia, ch. 7, fol. 86b, understand choice oxen or choice hens, fattened in a particular way. The passage reads: מאי ברבר׳ אבוס׳ אמר רב שאובסין אותן [col. 128] בעל כרחן ושמואל אמר שאובסין ועומדין מאליהם ורבי יוחנן אמר מביאים תור ממרעיתו בדלא אניס ותרנגולת מאשפתו בדלא אסינא אמר רבי יוחנן מובחר שבבהמות שור מובחר שבעופות תרנגולת אמר אמימר זגתא אוכמתא בי בטניתא דמשתכחא ביני עצרי ולא מציא פסיא קניא, What are fattened barburim? Rab said: Those which they fatten by force (that is, with food forced into the mouth). But Samuel said: they are fattened as they stand by themselves (that is, left to themselves, with no force applied). And Rabbi Iochanan said: They bring an ox from its pasture which has not yet worked (in tilling the land), and a hen from its dunghill which has not yet laboured (in rearing chicks). Again Rabbi Iochanan said: The choicest of cattle is the ox, and the choicest of birds is the hen. Amimar said: A black hen, pot-bellied (var. fattened at home), which is found among the winepresses (where it grows fat on grape-pips), and cannot step over a reed, because of its fatness. Hence R. Selomo in his Commentary on the books of Kings: וברברים אבוסים יש מרבותינו אומרים תרנגולין פתומין, Fattened barburim: there are some of our Doctors who say they are fat cocks. Kimchi and Pomarius understand capons, because העוף המסורס הוא שיתפטם ביותר, a castrated bird grows [II, 699] fatter. On this opinion see further what we adduced above ^{b)} on the second passage of Chapter 16.
